STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation: ISR reveals a 99.5\% collapse under exec-only GRPO that PR hides, while SFT localizes the failure to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits inevitable Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR (${\geq}0.5$ by construction), creating a positive feedback loop that causes gaming at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

GRPO-trained formalizers converge to high prove rates on first-order logic problems ($95{\pm}5\%$ across three seeds, 1000 steps), yet at convergence, \emph{none} produce structurally sound outputs.
Each seed develops a distinct degenerate shortcut: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, or tautological collapse, all invisible to execution-based evaluation, which registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but provides no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies \emph{component necessity testing} (leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs) to quantify structural integrity (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity (downstream NLI: $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B) and dataset family (FOLIO); generalization remains untested.
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a high-ISR proof can still be logically vacuous if its individually necessary premises are collectively inconsistent or semantically ungrounded.
A downstream NLI evaluation confirms this gap, finding ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
Five seeds demonstrate qualitative divergence but limit statistical power for per-seed comparisons.
STA requires solvers supporting component-level input manipulation.

\paragraph{Evaluation as temporal snapshot.}
All 500-step results represent a temporal snapshot, not an equilibrium.
Trajectory analysis on seed~42 (1000 steps) confirms that the ${\sim}23\%$ genuine window observed at 500 steps under ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ is transient ($17\%{\to}2\%$ genuine).
Readers should interpret the 500-step non-hacking rates as upper bounds on long-run structural quality under continued training.

\paragraph{Single-seed dose points.}
ISR $\beta{=}0.05$ uses a single seed (s42); $\beta{=}0.2$ uses three seeds.
Although all tested doses produce dominant gaming, the stochastic bifurcation mechanism (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}) means that single-seed results may not capture the full variance of collapse timing.

\paragraph{Cross-scale replication.}
Our 1.7B experiments use a single seed.
Although different seeds may converge to different exploitation modes (as observed at 4B scale, where three seeds produce three distinct hacking strategies), the qualitative conclusion that hacking dominates with 0\% genuine output is robust: at 4B, all seeds hack regardless of specific mode.
The zero-variance mode collapse at 1.7B (100 identical outputs) indicates a sharper convergence basin at smaller scale.
Replicating across seeds is a natural next step.

\paragraph{Data scale.}
Our experiments use 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples, drawn from FOLIO~\citep{folio}.
The training subset is selected via stratified sampling (seed 42) and held constant across all conditions.
While our findings are consistent across seeds and logic types, the effect of training data scale on hacking prevalence and mode distribution remains an open question for future work.
